summary: Provides shared terms and metrics for benchmarking sub-IP protection mechanisms, such as automatic protection switching, VRRP, stateful high availability and MPLS fast reroute. The results are measured at the IP layer. Other documents can use this vocabulary when they define test methods.

plainLanguage.summary: If a road breaks, a backup road can take over. This sets out the words and measurements to test how quickly and smoothly different backup systems for networks take over.

subtitle: Vocabulary and metrics for testing how quickly network backup systems take over when a failure occurs.

tldr.problem: Network protection mechanisms like VRRP, MPLS Fast Reroute, and automatic switching provide backup paths or redundant nodes when failures happen. Different technologies use different terms and measure success differently, making it hard to compare them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a common vocabulary for all sub-IP protection mechanisms: primary and backup paths, failover events, detection time, recovery time, and metrics like packet loss and delay. It covers five protection types (link, node, path, local link, and redundant node) and describes how to measure failover time using three methods.
tldr.outcome: Network operators and equipment vendors can now benchmark different protection technologies using a shared vocabulary, enabling fair comparison of performance across mechanisms.

today: RFC 6414 is an Informational document that establishes the terminology for benchmarking sub-IP layer protection mechanisms. It has not been obsoleted and is referenced by methodology documents for testing specific protection technologies like VRRP, MPLS-FRR, and Stateful HA.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
Network protection mechanisms operate at sub-IP layers to provide fast recovery from failures without waiting for IP-layer routing to converge. Examples include Automatic Protection Switching (APS) at the SONET/SDH layer, the Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP) for node redundancy, Stateful High Availability (HA) for stateful failover, and MPLS Fast Reroute for label-switched path protection. These mechanisms can provide recovery in tens to hundreds of milliseconds, much faster than IP routing convergence.

This document provides a single terminology framework for benchmarking all these protection mechanisms. The metrics are measured at the IP layer so results are independent of the specific protection technology. The goal is to enable methodology documents for different protection mechanisms to use consistent terms, allowing fair comparison across technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: Different technologies protect networks in different ways: some work by switching to a backup link, some by switching to a backup router, some at the MPLS label level. This sets out the words and measurements to test any of them fairly.

sections.title: Protection Paths and Elements
sections.content:
The core concept is a Primary Path (the normal route for traffic) and a Backup Path (activated when a failure occurs). The Headend Node is the entry point to the Primary Path, and the Merge Node is where the Backup Path rejoins the Primary Path. Between them may be midpoint nodes that could fail.

A Failover Event is a failure (link down, node down, timeout) that causes traffic to switch from Primary to Backup. The Point of Local Repair (PLR) is the node that detects the failure and initiates the switch. A backup path can protect at different granularities: Link Protection protects against a single failed link, Node Protection protects against a failed node, and Path Protection protects the entire Primary Path.

For node redundancy, a Primary Node (the active node) is protected by a Standby Node (the backup node). A State Control Interface may exchange session state between them so the Standby Node can take over with minimal data loss. The nodes may be adjacent or separated by multiple hops.
sections.plainLanguage: The normal path goes through certain routers (Headend to Merge Node). If something breaks, a backup path kicks in. The switch can protect just a broken link, just a broken router, or a whole stretch of the path. Or, a backup router takes over for the main router.

sections.title: Failure Detection and Recovery States
sections.content:
When a Failover Event occurs, a sequence of states follows. Failure Detection is the process of discovering that a failure has happened, using mechanisms like detecting a link-down event or timing out on a keepalive packet. Failover is the process of switching traffic from Primary to Backup. Failover is complete when no more packet loss, reordering, or duplication is observed on the Backup Path.

Restoration is the state where the Primary Path has recovered from the failure but is not yet carrying traffic. Reversion (optional) is the step where traffic switches back to the Primary Path after Restoration. During Reversion, the discontinuity in end-to-end delay between the Primary and Backup paths can cause out-of-order packets, duplicates, and increased jitter.
sections.plainLanguage: When a failure happens: detect it, switch traffic to the backup, wait for the broken link to be fixed, then optionally switch back. Each step takes time and can lose or scramble packets.

sections.title: Five Types of Protection
sections.content:
This document defines protection mechanisms across five categories. Link Protection provides a backup path when a link fails; the backup originates at the node before the failed link and rejoins after it. Node Protection protects against a node failure by routing around the failed node.

Path Protection provides a completely disjoint backup path from Headend to Merge Node, protecting against any combination of node or link failures along the Primary Path. Local Link Protection is a sub-IP mechanism that provides a backup between two nodes without a separate Backup Node, such as SONET APS automatically switching to a protection channel on the same fiber pair.

Redundant Node Protection (VRRP or HA) does not use a separate Backup Path. Instead, a Standby Node runs in parallel with or as hot standby for the Primary Node. Traffic continues along the same Primary Path through whichever node is active. This type is well-suited to protecting equipment at a single location.
sections.plainLanguage: Backup systems can protect just a broken link, a broken router, an entire path, two sides of one cable, or a redundant router. Each type is better in different situations.

sections.title: Metrics and Measurement
sections.content:
The key metrics for measuring protection performance are Failover Packet Loss (packets lost from the last unimpaired packet on Primary to the first unimpaired packet on Backup), Reversion Packet Loss (packets lost when switching back), Failover Time (duration of the failover process), and Reversion Time (duration of the reversion process). Additive Backup Delay measures the extra latency if the Backup Path is longer than the Primary Path.

Failover Time can be calculated using three methods. Time-Based Loss Method (TBLM) uses the tester's clock to measure the duration of packet loss. Packet-Loss-Based Method (PLBM) divides the number of lost packets by the offered load rate. Timestamp-Based Method (TBM), the recommended approach, embeds timestamps in packets and measures the interval between unimpaired packets, eliminating clock synchronization requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: To measure a backup system: count the packets lost during the switch and after, measure how long it takes to finish switching, and measure the delay difference if the backup path is longer. Three ways to measure time: use a clock, count packets, or use packet timestamps.

sections.title: Testing Considerations
sections.content:
Benchmarking tests must be conducted in a controlled laboratory environment with dedicated address space, not connected to production networks. The Protection-Switching System must include at minimum a Headend Node, a Merge Node, and either a pair of paths (Primary and Backup) or a pair of nodes (Primary and Standby). A tester outside the protection system sends traffic and records packet sequence numbers, departure and arrival times to compute loss and delay.

When measuring Failover Time using Timestamp-Based Method, the tester must record sequence numbers and timestamps in the packet payload. Unimpaired packets are those with correct sequence numbers (no loss, reordering, or duplication). A sequence gap indicates impaired packets. Testing should use at least 16 flows spread across the routing table to avoid missing prefix-specific behavior. Reversion, if tested, must be conducted after Restoration is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: To test a backup system: set up a fake network in a lab, send traffic through it, break something on purpose, watch how many packets are lost and how long the switch takes, then fix it and measure the switch back.
